sections.h2: How many days of notice does a Washington landlord have to give before an eviction?
sections.html:
It depends on the reason. For unpaid rent on a residential tenancy, the landlord must serve a written notice to pay or vacate and wait 14 days. For a lease violation other than rent, the wait is 10 days. For waste, a nuisance or an unlawful business, it is three days. These periods come from RCW 59.12.030, and the residential cause list in RCW 59.18.650 ties to them.

No court case can begin until the notice period has run without the tenant complying. If the landlord skips the notice or serves the wrong one, the later court filing is open to challenge. The state's rules also apply in the same way whether the landlord is an individual owner or an investor who wants to sell.

sections.h2: What are the main Washington eviction notice types and periods?
sections.html:
Washington residential landlords cannot end a tenancy without one of the causes written in RCW 59.18.650. The table lists the notice lengths that matter most to an owner who is trying to sell.

ReasonWritten noticeSource
Unpaid rent14 days to pay or vacateRCW 59.12.030(3)
Lease or rule violation other than rent10 days to fix it or vacateRCW 59.12.030(4)
Waste, nuisance or unlawful activity3 days to quitRCW 59.12.030(5), RCW 59.18.650(2)(c)
Owner or family moving in90 daysRCW 59.18.650(2)(d)
Owner selling a single-family home90 daysRCW 59.18.650(2)(e)
Home certified or condemned as unfit to live in30 daysRCW 59.18.650(2)(h)
Tenant shares a kitchen or bath with the owner20 daysRCW 59.18.650(2)(i)

sections.h2: What must a Washington 14-day pay or vacate notice say?
sections.html:
RCW 59.18.057 prescribes a form that must be used substantially as written. It lists unpaid rent, utilities and other recurring charges by month, shows a total amount due, and says where the money is to be paid. It also tells the tenant that payment must follow the rental agreement or be made by nonelectronic means such as a cashier's check or money order.

The notice must tell the tenant that any payment is applied first to the total on the notice. It must also describe resources: the Attorney General's website for rental help, the Eviction Defense Screening Line for qualifying low-income renters, the Northwest Justice Project CLEAR hotline, dispute resolution centers for low-cost mediation, and the right to an interpreter in court. A notice that leaves these out or demands more than the lease allows invites a defense.

  • List each month and each category separately.
  • Give a payment address and the owner or landlord name.
  • Sign and date the notice so the days can be counted.

sections.h2: How does a landlord serve an eviction notice in Washington?
sections.html:
RCW 59.12.040 allows three methods in order of preference. The first is handing a copy to the tenant in person. If the tenant is absent from the home, a copy can be left with a person of suitable age and discretion there, and a second copy is mailed to the tenant's residence. If the residence is not known or nobody suitable can be found, the landlord can post the notice in a conspicuous place on the property, give a copy to anyone living there, and mail a copy.

When service is by mail, it is complete on the day the copy goes into the mail from within Washington with postage paid, but five more days must pass before an action can be started on that notice. Any termination notice must also state the date by which the tenant has to vacate or, where it applies, comply.

The causes listed in RCW 59.18.650 require more. A notice under that section must be served the same way and must describe the facts known to the landlord at that time with enough detail for the tenant to prepare a response.

sections.h2: Can a Washington landlord end a tenancy because the house is being sold?
sections.html:
Yes, but only on the terms in RCW 59.18.650(2)(e). A tenant who stays after the owner elects to sell a single-family residence can be removed if the landlord gave at least 90 days' advance written notice of the date possession is to end. The owner is treated as electing to sell when the owner makes reasonable attempts within 30 days after the tenant leaves, and at a minimum lists the home at a reasonable price with a realty agency or on the multiple listing service.

There is a rebuttable presumption that the owner did not intend to sell if the home is not listed within 30 days of the tenant moving out. The same presumption applies if, within 90 days of the move-out or the listing date, whichever is later, the owner pulls the house off the market, rents it to someone else, or otherwise shows no intent to sell.

A fixed-term lease cannot be ended early on this ground. Subsection (5) says an owner may do that only with the tenant's written consent and at least 60 days for the tenant to vacate.

sections.h2: What happens if a landlord removes a tenant without following the rules?
sections.html:
A landlord who removes a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 is liable for wrongful eviction. The tenant who wins can recover the greater of their economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs. Changing the locks or removing belongings without a court order is the kind of act that sets this exposure in motion, so owners who want a vacant house for sale should wait for the process to end.

Washington also provides that an indigent tenant in an eviction case may have a court-appointed attorney, subject to available funding, according to the Attorney General's landlord-tenant page. Expect tenants to know that and to ask for it.

sections.h2: What should a Washington owner do next if a tenant will not leave a house that is for sale?
sections.html:
Count the notice period from the service date, keep proof of how the notice was delivered, and do not file anything in superior court before the period runs out. If the tenant pays in full within the notice period, the notice has been satisfied and the nonpayment case cannot go forward on that notice. Lease violations can be cured within 10 days of service.

When you are weighing a sale, compare timelines. A 90-day sale notice, then the court process described on our Washington eviction process page, can run for months. Some owners decide to sell the house with the tenant in place or to negotiate a move-out date in writing, which the statute allows for a fixed-term lease when the tenant agrees. A lawyer or the county superior court clerk can confirm local filing steps.

faqs.q: How long is a Washington eviction notice for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: It is 14 days for a residential tenancy. The landlord serves a written pay-or-vacate notice, and if the tenant does not pay or leave within 14 days after service, the landlord may file an unlawful detainer case.

faqs.q: Can a Washington landlord evict without a reason?
faqs.a: Generally no. RCW 59.18.650 says a landlord may not evict, refuse to continue a tenancy or end a periodic tenancy except for listed causes. Limited no-cause endings exist only for certain fixed-term leases with 60 days' notice.

faqs.q: How much notice does a Washington landlord give to sell the house?
faqs.a: At least 90 days' written notice for a single-family residence, and the owner must follow through by listing the home within 30 days after the tenant moves out. Otherwise there is a presumption that the owner never meant to sell.

faqs.q: How must a Washington eviction notice be delivered?
faqs.a: By personal delivery, by leaving a copy with a suitable person and mailing another, or, when neither is possible, by posting it on the property, giving a copy to a resident and mailing a copy. Mail service adds five days before a case can start.

faqs.q: What is the penalty for an illegal eviction in Washington?
faqs.a: A tenant who wins can recover the greater of actual damages or three times the monthly rent, plus attorneys' fees and court costs, under RCW 59.18.650(4).
